newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel poised for Hebron pullback.
newsitem.headline: Israel poised for Hebron pullback.

text.p: Israel's parliament voted overwhelmingly on Thursday to approve the Israel-PLO deal on Hebron, giving the green light for Israeli soldiers to pull out of much of the West Bank city.

To the cheers of Palestinians, the Israeli army dismantled bases and checkpoints in Hebron in preparation for a redeployment which Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai said would start after Knesset ratification of the U.S.-brokered accord.
Minutes after the vote, the head of the Palestinian Preventive Security agency, Jibril Rajoub, arrived at Israeli military headquarters in Hebron in a sign a handover was imminent.
"The building will immediately be handed over to us," a senior PLO police official said at the scene.
Hundreds of Arabs chanted nationalist slogans and waved Palestinian flags outside the headquarters, a symbol of an Israeli occupation that began after the 1967 Middle East war.
In Jerusalem, the 120-member parliament voted 87-17, with one abstention, to approve the Hebron deal and three further troop redeployments from mainly rural areas of the West Bank.
The accord, clinched after months of arduous negotiations, marked the first time the right-wing government had agreed to hand over territory Israel occupied in the 1967 Middle East war to PLO rule.
The main opposition Labour party and left-wing and Arab factions joined with most members of the ruling Likud coalition to ratify the accord after a 12-hour debate.

"I thank the members of the house, I hope in the future, during this government's term, to bring complete peace agreements with the Palestinians and perhaps with Arab nations, in addition to the ones we have signed," Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu told parliament.

"Today, after the Knesset's decision, the redeployment will begin," Mordechai told Israel Television, estimating that most of the pullback would be completed before the start of the Jewish sabbath on Friday evening.
"All activity related to redeployment will stop when the Sabbath begins and if something still needs to be completed, it will be done on Saturday night," he said.
Earlier on Thursday, a soldier pulled down a blue and white Star of David flag from the sentry box at the entrance to Hebron.
Israeli security sources said there would be little equipment left to take away once the green light to evacuate 80 percent of the city was given.

"We are not leaving Hebron, we are redeploying in Hebron," Netanyahu told parliament in Jerusalem. His remarks were aimed at right-wingers and Jewish settlers who staged a cabinet revolt against the accord sealed with Arafat.
Netanyahu muscled the accord through cabinet by an 11-7 majority after a stormy 12-hour meeting that ended on Thursday morning. Science Minister Binyamin Begin resigned in protest.
The prime minister held a televised prime-time news conference on Thursday evening to defend the deal.
He said the Hebron pullback commitment had been "inherited" from the previous Labour-led administration.
"I want to tell you what is not our way: we were not elected to retreat to the (pre-) 1967 (Middle East war) lines and establish a Palestinian state with Jerusalem as its capital," Netanyahu said.
Less than 48 hours after Israel and the PLO clinched a deal on Hebron, the sides differed on how additional Israeli pullbacks in the West Bank would be decided.

Netanyahu said in parliament a U.S. letter of guarantees stated Israel alone would define the scope of three further withdrawals from rural West Bank lands slated to follow the handover of most of Hebron to the Palestinians.
The PLO said it understood the depth of the pullbacks would be jointly determined.
Under U.S. documents accompanying the Hebron deal, the rural withdrawals agreed by Israel in a 1995 interim self-rule accord are due to start in March and be completed by mid-1998.
The U.S. State Department said on Wednesday Israel would define the depth of the future pullbacks.
Palestinian officials said 400 civilian and paramilitary police were poised to take over in Hebron. PLO sources said two busloads of Palestinian police had left self-ruled Jericho for Hebron.

Some 400 militant settlers live in the heart of Hebron. Another 5,000 live in fenced enclaves on the edge of this city of 100,000 Palestinians that contains the tomb of the biblical Abraham, a site revered by Jews and Moslems.
